Killer heart gene identified

By: Liz Fish | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
Heart muscle disease is effects 5 young South Africans on a daily basis. By studying rare illnesses like ARVC they develop cures for more common heart problems


Summary:
After 20 years of intense research a team of three woman at UCT’s medical school found that the genetic mutation of the gene called CDH2 is linked to a heart condition known as arythmogenic right ventricle cardiomyopathy- ARVC is commonly called Sudden Death syndrome. This cardiac disease kill’s very young people and tragically has claimed the lives of several young people in the same family. These young people often dropped dead without any obvious prior heart ailments. The significance of this discovery is the early detection of ARVC. The Medical Research Council says ARVC affects more than 5 young South Africans on a daily basis.


Further information:
Professor Bongani Mayosi Dean of UCT medical school started the research 20 years ago with one particular family who lost several siblings under the age of 25. He encouraged Dr Sarah Krause as part of her Phd to relook at the research using more advance non-invasive techniques. They tested over 145 families’ and found 62 had the disease. The big break- through came as a result in new genetic testing technique which Dr Gasnat Shoobadien learnt about while she was advancing her studies in Italy. Whole exome sequencing‚ can analyse every gene in a human's DNA. Prior to this it took 3 years to sequence one gene, now all 19000 genes can be analysed within days. Dr Shoobadien describes the technique as "genetics on steroids". CDH2 was identified as one of the 7 genes which can cause the illness which has been hailed as the biggest break through since Chris Barnard pioneered the first heart transplant 50 years ago.

This tiny team has made a breakthrough so significant that scientist from around the world are complimenting them on their findings. They sifted through 13000 variants and narrowed it down to CDH2.

Since the announcement was made many families have contacted the research team and have been placed on register to assist them in early detection and advance the research further because there is still so much we don’t know about ARVC.

Press Release:


Killer Heart Gene
It’s dubbed the biggest breakthrough since the first heart transplant in South Africa. A mystery of 20 years of intensive research has been cracked by a team of scientists at
UCT medical school. They’ve identified the killer gene linked to cardiac arrest in young adults. Carte Blanche meets the scientists behind this medical discovery.

Script:


Allan “He just packed an enormous amount into his day, sport, work whatever, he packed an enormous amount of effort into his day
Jenny “He actually happen to say to one of his friends, life is too short to say that it is too short. He achieved so much in his matric year, he was also doing the president’s award, he soared in his matric year. Prouder parents we could not have been. He looked so beautiful at his matric dance.
Script: The Baileys are a close knit family. Jenny and Allan are competitive athletes who shared their passion for sport with Steve. At 18 he was the top cross country runner at his school, he represented South Africa at the Maths Olympiad in Kazakhstan for which he was awarded a springbok blazer.
Bianca “I remember him helping me with my maths tutorial the night before and I remember saying don’t worry I don’t want to do it now we will do it tomorrow”
Link: “Steve parents were always concerned about his safety if fact Allan used to check his outside door every night but what they discovered the on the morning of the 19th of August they could never have imagined
Jenny “And then I walked into his room and I switched the light on and his face was in the pillow and jah I screamed beyond, I knew I knew, the paramedics did come and they did work on him for up to two hours they did everything humanly possible
Allan “My first thought was what could have happened to him he must have had a brain aneurism or something
Link “As avid soccer fans the Baileys may have heard about sudden cardiac deaths with several international players collapsing on the field but they would never have thought it would strike their own family
Allan “We knew he was exceptionally fit, but the two warning symptoms the first happened when he was about 14 and he fell in the bath and the GP came to pretty much the same conclusion that we did that the room was so full of steam that there wasn’t enough air in the room”
Script: Steve fainted again two years later, in hindsight this was the first indication of a rare heart condition
Link “ARVC or Arrythmogenic Right Ventricle Cardiomyopathy is a rare genetic heart disease and what makes it most tragic is that it usually effects young people”
Script: Professor Bongani Mayosi Dean of UCT Medical school, first started researching the condition 20 years ago when a family he was treating lost two siblings in short succession to ARVC and their two cousins were also affected. This year, they finally cracked the genetic code.
Bongani “Yes I am proud and relieved this was a project that seemed to be taking almost a life time to complete
Script: Despite many Phd students working on it over the years, and with extensive international collaboration, the research was painstaking.
Bongani “There were too few members of the family that were affected, the technology available at the time for identifying a genetic mutation in the family required that you had at least 10 members of the family that are affected “
Script: And in those days it took years to analyse one gene. Then in 2009 Genome sequencing blew the field of genetic research wide open says geneticist Dr Gasnat Shaboodien
Gasnat “You can screen 19 to 20 000 genes within a matter of hours.
Derek “You call it genetics on steroids”
Gasnat “I do call it genetics on steroids it really is it is fast and its quick. As humans we have 3 billion letters in our genetic code and we are looking for that one spelling error that can take us from a healthy individual to now having heart disease
Script : What the research team found was that the gene CDH2 which is linked to heart function and which we all have, mutates it causes disease to the heart muscle
Gasnat “What this gene does it links two heart cells together, so this is one heart cell and this is a heart cell and this is CDH2 and it links the heart cell together and if CDH2 doesn’t function properly you have the heart cells coming apart and you have the heart cells doing this, the current cannot pass from one heart cell to another”
Bongani “What happens in the heart you have an enlarged right side of the heart the theory is that as the cells loose contact they then die and in their place you get scar formation as well as fat cells and it is the scar and fat cells that is abnormal and causes the abnormal electrical activity in the heart and therefore leads to sudden death
Link: What this small team has discovered is a first in the world that will help the diagnosis and treatment of heart muscle disease in the future
Derek “Now this is just one genome in a cell which contains at least 19 000 genes
Gasnat “That’s right and this is the gene but we will still looking for one letter in that gene that was misspelt so your genetic code consists of ATCG the 4 bases and that little base is the spelling error that caused that whole disease within that family”
Script: When the news broke the Baileys contacted specialist physician Dr Sarah Kraus who works closely with the families.
Sarah “Sometimes there are no symptoms beforehand. I think that any young individual that has a fainting episode during sport should be looked at or should be taken seriously the only difficulty is that some of those screening tests might be negative so the ECG might be normal the MRI could even be normal and that is because the disease starts at a microscopic level “
Script: And ironically when the person is extremely athletic it accelerates the onset of sudden death
Jenny “He had seen the joy and the passion that we got out of exercise and we actually encouraged him and he was just so driven and he loved it so it never entered our minds
Sarah “At the moment in SA there isn’t really a platform for these families to be screened .Proffesor Mayosi has started a clinic here a long time ago which is a cardio genetics clinic and we have tried through research and the cardiac clinic at Groote Schuur try to build the service where we can screen family members
Script: Since the age of 14, Bianca has undergone numerous tests, ECG’s, MRI’s but no genetic testing as yet
Bianca “They haven’t found anything and I do have to go for follow up checks but it’s just routine.
Sarah “It’s very anxiety provoking, but now we can clearly show the family and test the individuals and say you have the condition or firstly you have the mutation which means you are at risk for developing the condition or no you don’t have the mutation so yes you can go and run that marathon or yes you can have children and not worry. If you have the condition and you are not showing signs of the disease we can plan a treatment strategy”
Link: It’s been heralded as the biggest breakthrough in SA cardiology since Doctor Chris Barnard very first heart transplant
Bongani “If we find a mechanism underlying sudden cardiac death and we can stop it then we would help a lot more people than for example heart transplantation this genetic mutation lies in a biological pathway that had not been associated with cardio myopathy before and revealing a new target …for the potential development of new drugs in the future
Derek “How was this news received internationally
Gasnat “It was phenomenal, I think it was bigger than we expected it to be. In SA it was even more amazing I was getting calls from spouses and fathers and mothers and one of their children and they were looking for answers to what had happened to their children
Allan “If your child one or two fainting episodes that don’t have obvious reasons you should at least have them checked out and have an ECG and to save the terrible tragedy we have been through it seems to me to be a no brainer really “
